slides.title: Everyday Leadership Techniques
slides.body: At your next practice, meeting or shift, try a five-minute huddle, notice one action worth repeating and follow up on one standard. You can practice all three without a management title.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Four chapters, one week of practice
slides.body: Part IV, Techniques of Leadership, covers Chapter 17, Constant Pressure; Chapter 18, One-on-One Leadership; Chapter 19, Document the Truth; and Chapter 20, 80% Affirmation / 20% Correction. Allow about 50 minutes. The huddle and difficult-conversation guides come from the book’s resources.
slides.aria: Four chapters, one week of practice
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: What happens after the announcement?
slides.body: Suppose your club agrees to put unused materials back on the supply table. At the end of the meeting, walk back to the table. Check whether people knew where supplies belonged and whether they had time to put them away. That return visit is part of setting the standard.
slides.quote: Standards are not announced. They are maintained.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 17: Constant Pressure
slides.notes: Add a person responsible for the next check and a time to do it.

slides.title: The busy day tests the standard
slides.body: Restaurant example (illustrative). On a short-handed shift, the lead still checks that the next station has its supplies. They ask which items are missing and help arrange a refill. In a club, the equivalent is checking that the next volunteer has the materials for their job. A calm, repeatable check makes the expectation dependable.
slides.aria: The busy day tests the standard
slides.quote: Constant pressure does not mean yelling. It does not mean intensity. It does not mean making people uncomfortable. It means consistency. It means that the standard is the same today as it was yesterday.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 17: Constant Pressure
slides.notes: Add a person responsible for the next check and a time to do it.

slides.title: Choose a standard you can revisit
slides.body: Think of something you asked a group to do. When did you last check whether it happened? Follow-up can be as small as asking at the next practice whether every ball made it back into the bag.
slides.aria: Choose a standard you can revisit
slides.quote: Issuing the order is only about five percent. The other ninety-five percent is ensuring it is carried out.
slides.source: George S. Patton, quoted in Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 17: Constant Pressure.
slides.fieldLabel: Write the standard in one sentence. Add when you’ll check it, what you’ll look for and what you can do if the group hits an obstacle.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Open with a five-minute huddle
slides.body: The book’s Pre-Shift Huddle Template has four parts. Set the tone. Name one priority. Recognize a specific person for a recent action. Invite input. For a volunteer table, the priority might be that every arriving helper knows their first job. Use spare time to answer an obstacle or confirm the handoff.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Write this week’s huddle
slides.body: Pick a shift, a pre-game gathering or a project meeting. Imagine everyone has only five minutes before they start. A useful opening ends with someone else getting to speak.
slides.fieldLabel: Fill four boxes on paper or in your draft: (1) one opening sentence, (2) the one thing the group should keep in mind, (3) a real action you can recognize, (4) one question that could surface a missing tool or unclear job. Read the huddle aloud.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Walkthrough A · Run the huddle
slides.body: Use the two practice scripts below. Listen for the moment a volunteer learns what to do first. Try delivering the four-part huddle yourself, then shorten any line that makes the priority hard to remember.
slides.notes: Follow the annotated demonstration and narration script. Pause where the learner is asked to try a step.

slides.title: Let people see what right looks like
slides.body: Affirmation means telling someone what they did well. Correction means helping someone adjust an action. The rough 80/20 rhythm reminds you to notice good work that often passes quietly. If something needs prompt correction, address it privately as soon as appropriate.
slides.aria: Let people see what right looks like
slides.quote: Eighty percent affirmation. Twenty percent correction. Not because correction is unimportant. But because people need to know what right looks like. Not just what wrong looks like.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 20: 80% Affirmation / 20% Correction
slides.notes: Ask which action the person would know to repeat.

slides.title: Describe the action worth repeating
slides.body: Compare two sample messages to a student volunteer. “Great job” shows appreciation. “When you showed the new helper where the spare bags were, they could restart the table on their own” also tells them what helped. Use what you actually saw.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 20: 80% Affirmation / 20% Correction
slides.notes: Ask which action the person would know to repeat.

slides.title: Practice three affirmations and one correction
slides.body: Look back at a practice or club meeting. One person may have made space for a quiet teammate to ask a question. Somebody else may have checked that a new member understood the task. Notice contributions that are easy to miss.
slides.aria: Practice three affirmations and one correction
slides.quote: This works because it aligns with reality. In a typical shift, correction will happen naturally. Problems will surface automatically. You do not need a reminder to fix things. You need a reminder to build people.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 20: 80% Affirmation / 20% Correction
slides.fieldLabel: Draft three specific, earned affirmations. For each, name the action and whom it helped. Then describe one behavior you would address privately and one expectation you would explain. Use roles or fictional examples.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Look up every eight to ten minutes
slides.body: During a practice or shift, pause when the next interval comes around. Look across the room, find an action that helped and name it while the person remembers it. The book’s practice is every 8–10 minutes. The optional app lets users set intervals of 8–15 minutes. A clock or ordinary timer works for the exercise.
slides.aria: Look up every eight to ten minutes
slides.quote: Every eight to ten minutes, a leader should look up, observe the team, identify something done right, and say it out loud.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 20: 80% Affirmation / 20% Correction
slides.notes: Ask which action the person would know to repeat.

slides.title: Optional next step · Leadership Rhythm
slides.body: Optional next step: Leadership Rhythm is a free iPhone and iPad app (App Store, rated 4+) that uses timed intervals to prompt you to notice and recognize people during a shift or practice. Brenen built it to go with Chapter 20 of the book. You do not need it to finish this class. If you use an iPhone or iPad with iOS or iPadOS 16.4 or later and you want a reminder to look up and notice what someone is doing right, you can find it on the App Store.
slides.notes: A clock, a timer or a paper reminder also works. Always offer the no-app path.

slides.title: Catch the small moment
slides.body: A group announcement is useful when everyone needs the same information. If one teammate is missing a handoff, ask for a short conversation after practice. Describe the specific handoff while you both remember it. Give them time to explain what happened.
slides.quote: Real leadership does not happen in meetings. It happens in moments. One-on-one. Face to face. In the middle of the work.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 18: One-on-One Leadership
slides.notes: Keep a routine correction private. Take serious harm to the responsible adult.

slides.title: Correct with dignity
slides.body: Ask to speak out of earshot in a suitable setting, following your school or workplace rules. Someone can hear a direct request more easily when their teammates are not an audience. If your own words slipped in the group chat, acknowledge that and take the individual conversation private.
slides.source: Danny Meyer, quoted in Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 18: One-on-One Leadership.
slides.notes: Keep a routine correction private. Take serious harm to the responsible adult.

slides.title: The Marcus field story · Speak early
slides.body: The lesson from the Marcus field story is to make expectations clear while the other person still has a chance to act on them. For a student project, that means speaking up when the first agreed handoff is missed and making time to hear why.
slides.aria: The Marcus field story · Speak early
slides.quote: Never let someone fail in silence. If expectations are not spoken clearly, they are not being led.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 18: One-on-One Leadership, field-story Manager Rule.
slides.notes: Keep a routine correction private. Take serious harm to the responsible adult.

slides.title: Five steps for a difficult conversation
slides.body: Use the book’s Difficult Conversation Guide. 1. Choose a calm, private setting. 2. State the facts and the effect on the work. 3. Name a specific expectation and ask for a commitment. 4. Listen for an obstacle. 5. Explain the real, appropriate next step if the issue continues. Stay within your role. A student can ask the advisor to help reassign a task. A student cannot fire a classmate.
slides.aria: Five steps for a difficult conversation
slides.quote: When it is time to address a performance or behavior issue, follow this structure. Have the conversation in private, never in front of the team.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Difficult Conversation Guide (resource for Chapter 18: One-on-One Leadership).
slides.notes: Keep a routine correction private. Take serious harm to the responsible adult.

slides.title: Check your posture before you speak
slides.body: Before a routine feedback conversation, answer each question below. If any answer is unclear, take another minute to prepare. For harassment, discrimination, violence or a safety issue, get help from a trusted adult, advisor or manager. Students should never have to resolve those situations alone.
slides.aria: Check your posture before you speak
slides.quote:
Am I seeking to help, or seeking to be right?
Am I addressing the behavior, not attacking the person?
Have I prepared specific facts, not just feelings?
Am I giving a clear path forward, not just pointing out the problem?
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Difficult Conversation Guide (resource for Chapter 18: One-on-One Leadership).
slides.notes: Keep a routine correction private. Take serious harm to the responsible adult.

slides.title: Draft a private conversation
slides.body: Choose one fictional situation. A club supply kit reached the check-in table ten minutes after opening. Or a teammate handed over their section after the group’s agreed editing deadline. Pick only the facts you know. Leave room for an explanation.
slides.quote: That is the standard. Correction should clarify, guide, and improve. Not diminish. Not embarrass. Not shut someone down.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 18: One-on-One Leadership
slides.fieldLabel: Write five short lines: where you’ll speak; what you observed and its impact; what you’re asking for; one question you’ll ask and then wait to hear answered; what you can actually do if the issue continues. Read it once through the other person’s ears.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Walkthrough B · A private handoff conversation
slides.body: Follow the sample dialogue from the first factual sentence to the follow-up agreement. Pause before reading the teammate’s answer. Try asking a question that would help you find out what made the handoff difficult.
slides.aria: Walkthrough B · A private handoff conversation
slides.notes: Follow the annotated demonstration and narration script. Pause where the learner is asked to try a step.

slides.title: Mid-class check
slides.body: Answer three practice questions about a huddle, earned affirmation and private correction. Read the explanation for each response, then return to any technique you want to rehearse.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Give both people a clear record
slides.body: After a conversation, write a short record of the agreement if it is appropriate for your role. You might send your project partner a shared task reminder that both of you can correct. At work, follow the manager’s official process for any record.
slides.aria: Give both people a clear record
slides.quote: Documentation is not about building a case against someone. It is not about being corporate or cold. It is about clarity to both the manager and the employee.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 19: Document the Truth
slides.notes: Separate a dated observation from an opinion about character.

slides.title: Write what you could verify together
slides.body: A useful project note might read: Thursday’s kit reached the table at 4:10. For Saturday, we agreed to put the kit beside the printed signs by 8:45. I’ll check at 8:40 whether the storage room is open. Include dates, observed facts and the agreement. Keep personal judgments, private details and classmates’ names out of practice notes. Never build secret files on peers or post corrections in a group chat.
slides.aria: Write what you could verify together
slides.quote: A conversation that is not documented can disappear.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 19: Document the Truth
slides.notes: Separate a dated observation from an opinion about character.

slides.title: Put the techniques in working order
slides.body: Before the meeting, run the huddle. During the work, look up and affirm a specific action. If a standard slips, speak privately when appropriate. Afterward, record the agreement through the right channel. At the next meeting, check whether it worked. That last visit closes the loop.
slides.aria: Put the techniques in working order
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Describe something you actually did
slides.body: If it happened, a resume bullet could read: Opened each volunteer shift with a five-minute huddle so new helpers knew their first job. Use a result you observed. If you have only practiced a script, keep the draft for later and come back after trying it.
slides.fieldLabel: Draft an action and its real result. What did you do? Who used it? What changed that you could explain in an interview? Leave out any title, figure or result you cannot support.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Worksheet · My Techniques Card
slides.body: Download the card and keep it on your own device. It holds a four-part huddle, an affirmation log, a private conversation and a follow-up note. Use roles or fictional examples. The final line about trying a timer or the app is optional.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Spot four ways a good intention can go wrong
slides.body: A long speech can bury the one priority. Vague praise can leave someone unsure what to repeat. A correction posted to the group can embarrass one person. A note written in anger can turn into accusations. Choose one of these and rewrite it as something you would be willing to say to the person involved.
slides.aria: Spot four ways a good intention can go wrong
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Four chapters to carry into your next meeting
slides.body: Chapter 17, Constant Pressure: check the same standard again. Chapter 18, One-on-One Leadership: keep individual correction private. Chapter 19, Document the Truth: record facts and agreements. Chapter 20, 80% Affirmation / 20% Correction: name good work people can repeat.
slides.aria: Four chapters to carry into your next meeting
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: When the whole group starts slipping
slides.body: A private check-in can help with an individual handoff. If every handoff is messy, examine the routine the whole group uses. The next class, When the Team Is Off Track, follows Chapters 21–23 through diagnosis, who leads each shift and how to repeat a written standard.
slides.aria: When the whole group starts slipping
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Optional completion record
slides.body: After passing the final, you can preview the completion line Everyday Leadership Techniques — completed on FirstCareerSteps. Choose whether it belongs on your resume. A completion record describes a class you took. It does not establish that you have supervised a team.
slides.notes: The student chooses whether to preview and confirm an addition.

slides.title: Practice case 1 · The unchanged supply table
slides.body: Ungraded rehearsal. A club has announced twice that the supply table should be reset after meetings. The same items are still left loose each week. Find the missing follow-up.
slides.aria: Practice case 1 · The unchanged supply table
slides.fieldLabel: Write the one action you will check, a time to check it and how you will ask whether the reset can be done with the available time and supplies.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Practice case 2 · A message to the whole team
slides.body: Ungraded rehearsal. A group-chat draft says that people who keep missing the handoff need to take the project seriously. You know the latest issue involved just one handoff. Decide who actually needs which information.
slides.aria: Practice case 2 · A message to the whole team
slides.quote: Not public correction. Not general announcements. Not passive-aggressive hints. Direct, honest, individual conversation.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Chapter 18: One-on-One Leadership
slides.fieldLabel: Draft a neutral reminder for everyone only if they need it. Then write the opening to a separate private conversation about the specific handoff.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Practice case 3 · A note both people can use
slides.body: Ungraded rehearsal. After a check-in, a draft note reads: The helper obviously does not care. You saw the supplies arrive ten minutes after opening, and you both agreed to meet at the storage room before the next event.
slides.aria: Practice case 3 · A note both people can use
slides.quote: If something matters enough to correct, it usually matters enough to write down.
slides.source: Brenen Morse, The Little Black Book on Leadership, Quick Reference for Chapter 19: Document the Truth.
slides.fieldLabel: Rewrite the note using the observed timing, your agreement and when you will check back. Remove the guess about the helper’s attitude.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Practice case 4 · Name a contribution
slides.body: Ungraded rehearsal. At practice, one teammate quietly set out the cones in the order the new players needed them. The coach saw a drill start without the usual search for equipment. Praise like “you’re amazing” leaves the useful action out.
slides.fieldLabel: Write one earned affirmation. Mention what the teammate did and how it helped. Say it as you would on the field.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Practice case 5 · A reminder goes off
slides.body: Ungraded rehearsal. It is ten minutes into a busy event. Your reminder sounds just as someone asks for help carrying a box. Help with the immediate need, then look up and notice the room.
slides.aria: Practice case 5 · A reminder goes off
slides.fieldLabel: What might you genuinely observe once the box is down? Write a conditional example. If you have not seen the action, wait until you have something real to recognize.
slides.notes: Give the learner time to try the prompt on paper or in the open tab. Examples may be fictional.

slides.title: Rehearsal debrief
slides.body: Compare your five responses. Can another person tell what happened, what they can do and when you will follow up? Could the person whose work you described read your note and recognize the facts? The next five slides form one final quiz. Four correct answers complete the class, and you can retry.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Final 1 · Maintain a standard
slides.body: Choose the answer that follows the chapter’s practice.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final 2 · Correct privately
slides.body: Choose the answer that follows the chapter’s practice.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final 3 · Document the truth
slides.body: Choose the answer that follows the chapter’s practice.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final 4 · Recognize good work
slides.body: Choose the answer that follows the chapter’s practice.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Final 5 · Look up and notice
slides.body: Choose the answer that follows the chapter’s practice.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Review your final answers
slides.body: Read the reason for each response. You can return to any chapter and retry the five questions as often as you need. A score of four out of five completes the class.
slides.notes: After an attempt, discuss the explanation and invite the learner to revisit the example.

slides.title: Put your Techniques Card where you’ll use it
slides.body: Take your downloaded card to the next club meeting, practice or shift. Circle the one priority for the huddle and write down when you’ll follow up. If the card contains personal reflections, keep it private.
slides.aria: Put your Techniques Card where you’ll use it
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

slides.title: Try the technique this week
slides.body: Run one short huddle. Follow it with one individual conversation: name an action someone should repeat or address one missed standard privately. Afterward, write the next date you’ll check the agreement.
slides.notes: Use the student example on this slide and allow a quiet moment to apply it to school, a club or work.

mid.prompt: You have five minutes before a club event. Which huddle gives the team the clearest start?
options: Name one shared priority, recognize a recent action and invite one obstacle.
List every possible job and tell people to remember all of them.
Spend the whole five minutes reminding everyone to stay positive.
mid.why: A single priority helps people make the same decision when things get busy. Recognition and a question make the huddle useful in both directions.

mid.prompt: During practice, you have mostly spoken up about mistakes. What would Chapter 20 have you do?
options: Give general praise each time you correct someone.
Look for specific actions worth repeating and describe them while they are fresh.
Let every mistake pass until you have counted four compliments.
mid.why: The 80/20 rhythm asks you to look deliberately for good work. Earned affirmation shows others exactly what to repeat. Handle a needed correction when it arises.

mid.prompt: A teammate keeps missing an agreed handoff. Why speak with them privately?
options: So nobody will know the standard exists.
So you can list everything they have ever done wrong.
So you can name the behavior, hear their side and agree on a change with dignity.
mid.why: One-on-one feedback gives the teammate room to answer. You can explain the shared standard to the whole group without identifying or embarrassing anyone.

final.prompt: “Standards are not announced. They are maintained.” means:
options: You only need to say the rule once.
Follow-up and consistency are the work, not the speech.
Yelling maintains the standard.
Standards should change with your mood.
final.why: Chapter 17 puts the work in what happens after you speak. Check that the expectation is understood and return to it the next time it matters.

options: In the group chat so everyone learns.
Through hints until they figure it out.
One-on-one, in private, with dignity.
Only after a formal meeting.
final.why: A private exchange lets you describe one action, hear the other person and make a useful agreement.

final.prompt: Chapter 19 treats writing things down as:
options: Building a case against someone.
Clarity and fairness for both people, so no one is shocked later.
Optional if you have a good memory.
Something to post publicly.
final.why: A short factual record helps both people remember what was asked, what they agreed and when they will check back.

options: 80% correction, 20% praise.
80% affirmation, 20% correction, so people also see what right looks like.
80% meetings, 20% work.
Ignoring mistakes.
final.why: Specific recognition makes good work visible. Targeted correction still has a place.

options: A required use of a paid app.
Looking up, noticing something done right, and saying it out loud.
Checking your phone.
A substitute for ever correcting anyone.
final.why: Chapter 20 describes observing and naming a real action. A clock, a simple timer or the optional Leadership Rhythm app can remind you.

walkthroughs.title: Run a huddle people can use
steps: Set up the rehearsal

Use the fictional volunteer check-in table in the script. Give yourself five minutes, a blank piece of paper and four headings: tone, priority, recognition, input. The huddle must end before the first helpers arrive.
Try the crowded opening
Read the first opening in the script aloud. Cover it and try to say what to do first. The speaker has given people a list without deciding what matters most.
Choose one job for the team
Put one priority on the page: every arriving volunteer should know their first assignment. A tidy table supports the goal, but arranging pens is not a second priority.
Deliver the four-part version
Read the revised huddle aloud. Pause after inviting input as you would in the room. Let the volunteer raise the missing assignment list, then decide who can check it before opening.
Practice, then listen back

Use two minutes to adapt the four headings to your own setting and one minute to deliver them. Ask a partner to repeat the priority or write it from memory yourself. If two priorities come back, shorten the opening.
narration: Practice script for a fictional club event.
Narrator: The first volunteers arrive in five minutes. Listen to this opening, then see whether you could tell a new helper what matters most.
Lead, first version: “We need the pens in order, a tidy entrance, everyone smiling, people signed in and bags put away. Let’s all do everything better than last time. Okay, let’s go.”

Narrator: Look away from the script. What should you choose if a new volunteer is waiting while the pens are scattered? The lead never made that decision clear. Cross out the list and write one priority: every arriving volunteer knows their first job.

Lead, revised version: “Thanks for coming early. We have five minutes together before we open. Our priority today is that every volunteer leaves this table knowing their first assignment. At our practice setup, the supplies helper put a picture of each kit beside the bins. That helped the new helpers pick one up without waiting for me. What could get in our way when the first people arrive?”
Volunteer: “The first-job list is still in the classroom. I have the pictures but I don’t know which kit goes with which job.”
Lead: “Thanks for catching that. I’ll ask the advisor for the list now. Could you keep the job cards beside their matching kits? When I get back, we’ll walk through the first arrival together.”

Narrator: Circle the moment the volunteer told us something the lead didn’t know. The pause matters. A huddle that never leaves time for an answer loses a chance to fix a problem before the rush. Read the revised opening once more, leaving a real pause.

Your rehearsal: Write four short lines of your own. Use a real example of good work, or label a practice example as imaginary. Give yourself two minutes to prepare, then a minute to say it aloud. End by asking for one obstacle and waiting. Can a new helper repeat the priority in one sentence?

walkthroughs.title: A private conversation about a late handoff
steps: Set the boundary

This fictional case is about a missing supply kit. Both students agreed to a handoff time. Use an appropriate private setting. Violence, harassment, discrimination or safety concerns belong with a trusted adult, advisor or manager.
Practice an opening
Read only the opening exchange. Write down the two observable facts and the effect on the welcome table. Cross out any guesses about motives. Try it once with a partner or read both parts yourself.
Ask and listen
Pause after asking what happened. Allow the teammate’s explanation to change the plan. Read the exchange and underline the new information about the storage room.
Make a realistic agreement

Compare the expectation before and after listening. Name what each person can actually do, when to ask the advisor for help and when to check back. A student peer has no authority to impose a school penalty.
Write a brief follow-up
Draft two sentences the teammate could read and correct. Include the fact, the next action and the follow-up time. Use no real names or private details.
Debrief your posture

Spend a minute asking whether your opening helped, described behavior, used facts and gave a path forward. Then spend two or three minutes swapping roles or repeating the exchange with a different obstacle.
narration: Practice dialogue. These are fictional club members working on a supply-table handoff.

Narrator: The club agreed the check-in kit would be ready by four. On two occasions the first helpers reached the table before the kit did. The person running the table asks the kit helper to talk after the event, away from the group. Read each exchange slowly, then rehearse it in your own words.
Table lead: “Is now a good time for a two-minute check-in about the supply kit? We can talk by the empty end of the table.”
Kit helper: “Yes.”

Table lead: “On Tuesday and Thursday the kit got to the check-in table at 4:10. We agreed to have it there at four. The first helpers waited while I found blank paper. Next time, I’d like the kit at the table before opening. What got in the way?”
Kit helper: “The storage room was locked. I waited for the advisor. I figured the table had spare paper until I got there.”
Narrator: Pause. Which part of the issue can the helper change? Which part needs someone with a key? Try answering the helper without guessing how much they care.

Table lead: “Thanks. I didn’t know the room was locked. For Saturday, can you meet me at the storage room at 8:40? I’ll check with the advisor ahead of time about access. If the door is locked, please tell me right away so we can ask the advisor for the kit together.”
Kit helper: “I can do 8:40. Can we keep a few blank sheets at the table in case we have to wait again?”

Table lead: “Yes. I’ll put them in the welcome folder. If we still can’t get the kit there by opening, we’ll ask the advisor to help change the handoff. I’ll check with you right after the first helpers arrive on Saturday. Does that sound right?”
Kit helper: “Yes. I’ll meet you at the storage room and let you know right away if it’s still closed.”

Narrator: Use a minute to write a note both people could recognize. A sample: “The kit arrived at 4:10 Tuesday and Thursday. For Saturday we agreed to meet at 8:40 at the storage room. I’ll confirm access with the advisor and bring spare sheets. We’ll check back after the first arrivals.” In a real job, use the approved workplace process. Do not create a file on a classmate.

One-minute posture debrief: First, were you trying to help? The lead took responsibility for arranging access. Second, was the conversation about behavior? It stayed with the arrival of the kit. Third, did you use facts? The two dates and the agreed time could be checked. Fourth, was there a path forward? Both people left with a job, a time and someone to ask if access failed.

Rehearse again: Swap roles or speak the other side yourself. Imagine the kit was complete but waiting at the wrong table. Take two or three minutes to listen and agree on one visible change. Keep any consequence within your role.
